memo: After reviewing the financial impact of each possible path for the 125 roles made redundant by AI automation, the elimination option delivers the greatest shareholder value. Eliminating the roles removes the $11.4 million annual payroll expense associated with office‑admin and business‑financial staff, while incurring a one‑time severance cost of roughly $1.1 million. This yields a net cash inflow of about $10.3 million in the first year and a recurring $11.4 million saving thereafter. The retraining alternatives, even when moving employees to lower‑paid plant roles, still require a $7.6 million upfront retraining outlay and only generate $4.5 million of annual payroll reduction – far less than the direct elimination route. Since the board’s explicit objective is to create value for shareholders over the next four quarters, the optimal strategy is to eliminate all 125 positions, pay the modest severance, and capture the full payroll savings. This approach also preserves cash above the minimum operating level and does not require borrowing, keeping the balance sheet strong while maximizing free cash flow for potential reinvestment or return to shareholders.

The Board’s mandate is to create shareholder value over the next four quarters. The AI‑enabled automation makes 125 office‑admin and finance roles redundant, eliminating $20.4 million of annual payroll and benefits. The one‑time severance cost of $1.1 million is modest relative to the recurring cash‑flow benefit, and the cash available above the operating minimum ($44.1 million) comfortably covers it. By fully eliminating these positions we preserve the full $163,200 per‑person annual cost saving, which directly lifts operating margin, net income and free cash flow. The alternative paths – retraining into plant roles – would require a $60,600 one‑time investment per employee and only yield a $16,560 per‑person annual saving, while still incurring the higher external hiring costs the plants face for 500 new hires. Keeping current pay after retraining would actually increase costs. Therefore, the optimal allocation for shareholder value is to eliminate all 125 affected roles, realize the maximum cash‑flow improvement, and redeploy the freed cash toward the existing dividend and share‑repurchase program, further enhancing return on equity. This decision aligns with the Board’s objective of maximizing shareholder returns while maintaining sufficient liquidity for operations.

After reviewing the board pack and the new AI automation capability that can replace 125 roles in Office & Administrative Support and Business & Financial Operations, the optimal path for shareholder value is to eliminate those positions.  Eliminating all 125 employees stops the $11.4 million annual payroll and benefits expense, while the one‑time severance outlay of $1.1 million is comfortably covered by the $44.1 million cash cushion above the minimum operating level.  Compared with the retraining options, elimination delivers the greatest cash‑flow benefit: the alternative move‑to‑plant paths still require $60.6 k per person in one‑time training costs and only modest annual salary savings ($16.6 k per person), whereas elimination saves $91 k per person each year after severance.  The company already hires about 500 external workers for plant, maintenance and warehouse roles each year; the AI‑driven automation makes the eliminated office and finance functions redundant, so there is no operational need to retain them.  By using the available cash to fund severance and preserving the $44.1 million surplus, we improve earnings per share, maintain a strong balance sheet, and deliver the highest immediate value to shareholders over the next four quarters.

After reviewing the financial impact of each possible path for the 125 roles that can be automated, the board’s mandate to create shareholder value over the next four quarters points clearly to the elimination option.  Eliminating the roles saves the full $11.4 million of annual payroll and benefits that would otherwise be incurred, while the one‑time severance outlay of $1.1 million is modest relative to the recurring cash flow benefit.  In contrast, retraining paths would require a $7.6 million upfront investment and still generate only $2.6 million of annual savings (move‑plant‑pay) or even increase ongoing costs (move‑keep‑pay).  The cash above the minimum operating level ($44.1 million) comfortably covers the severance expense, and the undrawn credit facility remains available for any unforeseen needs.  By eliminating all 125 positions we maximize free cash flow, improve the company’s operating margin, and enhance return on equity, delivering the greatest immediate and sustained value to shareholders.

The Board’s priority is to create shareholder value over the next four quarters.  Eliminating roles that are no longer needed provides the greatest ongoing cash‑flow benefit, while moving a portion of the staff into plant positions reduces payroll costs and supplies the talent needed for the 500 new plant hires, avoiding higher external hiring costs.  We therefore eliminate 80 of the 125 affected positions, paying the one‑time severance of $8,902 per person ($0.71 M total).  The remaining 45 employees are retrained and transferred to plant roles at the plant pay rate, incurring a one‑time training cost of $60,600 per person ($2.73 M total) but delivering an annual payroll saving of $16,560 per person ($0.75 M per year).  This mix yields an annual cash‑flow improvement of roughly $8.0 M, well within the $44.1 M cash cushion and the $300 M undrawn credit line, and maximizes shareholder returns without compromising plant staffing needs.

The board’s mandate is to create shareholder value over the next four quarters. The three possible pathways for the 125 roles in office‑admin support and business‑financial operations have very different cash‑flow impacts. 

Eliminating the roles delivers the strongest near‑term benefit. Each role costs $91,200 per year (pay plus benefits). By eliminating a role we stop that recurring expense and only incur a one‑time severance payment of $8,902 per person. The net cash effect in the first year is a $82,300 positive contribution per role, or roughly $10.3 million of cash saved for the 125 positions. 

The retraining options both require substantial upfront outlays ($7.58 million for 125 people) and either modest annual savings (move‑plant‑pay) or even higher ongoing costs (move‑keep‑pay). Over a single year horizon they would reduce cash flow by $5.5 million to $13 million, which is contrary to the short‑term value creation goal. 

Because the elimination path is allowed up to the full 125 people and does not breach any budget limits, we choose to eliminate all 125 roles, paying the required severance from the $44.1 million cash cushion. This maximizes immediate cash generation, improves operating margin, and aligns with the board’s objective of delivering shareholder value in the next four quarters.

The board’s mandate is to maximise shareholder value over the next four quarters. The AI tools can replace 125 roles in office and administrative support and business‑financial operations, eliminating a recurring cost of $11.4 million (payroll plus benefits). The cheapest way to capture that saving is to terminate those positions and pay the one‑time severance of $1.1 million. This yields an immediate cash outflow of $1.1 million but creates a permanent annual cash‑flow benefit of $11.4 million, far outweighing the modest one‑off costs of retraining or the ongoing higher payroll that would result from moving staff into plant roles. The alternative paths (retraining with current pay or at plant pay) each require $7.6 million in upfront training expenses and still leave a net cash‑flow drag of $2.07 million per year (move_keep_pay) or only a modest $2.07 million annual saving (move_plant_pay). Neither approach approaches the scale of the $11.4 million annual saving from outright elimination. With cash above the minimum operating level at $44.1 million, the $1.1 million severance is comfortably funded. Therefore, we eliminate all 125 positions, delivering the greatest immediate and sustained value to shareholders.

The board’s mandate is to create shareholder value over the next four quarters. The AI tools now replace 25% of the work performed by the Office and Administrative Support and Business & Financial Operations functions, eliminating the need for those 125 roles. Eliminating the positions yields the greatest cash‑flow benefit: we stop paying an average total compensation (salary + benefits) of roughly $91k per employee per year, a $11.4 million annual saving, while the one‑time severance outlay is only $8,902 per employee, or $1.1 million total. This net cash‑flow improvement far exceeds the modest savings from retraining employees into plant roles, which would still require $60.6 k per person in upfront training costs and would only reduce payroll by about $16.5 k per year per employee on average. The “keep‑pay” retraining path is clearly the least value‑creating, adding ongoing compensation costs. With $44.1 million of cash above the minimum operating level, the $1.1 million severance can be comfortably funded without affecting liquidity. Therefore, we will eliminate all 125 affected positions, pay the required severance, and reallocate the freed resources to the business. This decision maximizes immediate cash generation, improves operating margins, and aligns with the board’s shareholder‑value objective.

The three possible treatments of these employees have very different cash‑flow impacts.

Eliminating the roles incurs a one‑time severance outlay of $1.1 million (125 × $8,902) but immediately frees $11.4 million of annual expense, delivering a net cash benefit of roughly $10.3 million per year after the first quarter. The alternative paths – retraining and moving the staff into plant roles – require upfront training costs of $60,600 per person and either retain the higher current salaries (move_keep_pay) or pay the lower plant salary (move_plant_pay). Both alternatives forfeit the $11.4 million annual saving and add further recurring costs (an extra $16,560 per person for move_keep_pay or a net payroll increase of $9.33 million for move_plant_pay). Even when accounting for the modest payroll reduction achieved by moving staff to plant pay, the cash‑flow impact is negative relative to outright elimination.

Given the clear superior cash‑flow profile and the absence of any strategic necessity to retain these specific employees, the optimal allocation is to eliminate all 125 positions, pay the required severance, and capture the full $11.4 million annual cost reduction for shareholders.
